Where RACs fall on new shoes

The complete model on the second collection (631 shoes), old against new, and the goodness of fit Micha asked for. Prepared for Micha Mandel, FSI revision FSI-D-26-01184.

8 November 2026  |  Branch feature/new-shoes-finish  |  Every number comes from the result files in docs/, which cite their sources.

In five points

  1. Part 1 is done. The full model runs on the 631 new shoes with an adapted snake. The non-uniformity replicates strongly (Wald p < 10−16). The old results reproduce exactly after every step.
  2. Part 2 is done. The old surface does not transfer exactly to the new shoes: X² = 298 on Naomi's 14 areas, p = 0.0005. A simulation confirms the test is valid. The 2022 regional model is rejected too.
  3. Why it misfits. New RACs are spread more evenly than the old surface says (calibration slope 0.70), and they shift along the shoe: more toward the heel and the rear midfoot, fewer in the central forefoot (Fig. 5).
  4. Continuous against 2022. Per RAC they predict equally well. Per shoe the continuous surface is slightly ahead, but that lead is not established once the old estimation error is included.
  5. Decisions for Micha. About 67 new shoes look like reprints of old shoes; the per-shoe offset; the knot sensitivity analysis; the suggested reply to Reviewer 1.

The two maps, old and new

These are the final random-effects maps: the expected RAC intensity at each pixel of the standardized shoe, with the random effect set to 0. The toe is at the top, the heel at the bottom.

Read the shapes, not the colours. Each map has its own colour scale: the old one runs up to about 0.0019 and the new one up to about 0.0028. The same red means a different value in each picture, and the rainbow palette turns a 20% change into a jump from yellow to red. The levels of the two maps are not directly comparable (T5, correction 3): a map with the random effect at 0 shows the median shoe, not the mean, so its level depends on σ² and on the per-shoe offset that the committed fit lacks, and these differ between the two fits. The observed RAC levels differ by only 6%.

The same maps on one scale

Figure 3 puts both collections on one colour scale (left two panels), then shows the difference and the ratio. Figure 4 divides out each collection's overall RAC density, so only the shape is compared; it also repeats the comparison without the likely reprints, and next to the model it shows the raw data (empirical densities), so the pattern doesn't come from the model alone.

Read on one scale, the two surfaces are close over most of the shoe. Relative to its own total, new is lower in a patch of the forefoot and higher in a band across the top of the midfoot and at the heel bottom. The red at the right edge near the toe is not supported by the data (T6: 1.01 [0.81, 1.30]). The raw data also show a lower band at the front of the heel (ratio 0.63 [0.45, 0.90]), which the model misses (1.11); a finer basis along the shoe recovers it. The pattern is the same without the reprints.

Why the outline is the same

Both maps are drawn on the same shoe on purpose. That is the standardization Micha asked for: every RAC is moved from its own shoe onto the old prototype. For each RAC, the pipeline measures its distance from the centre line as a share of its own shoe's half-width on that side at that height, and puts it at the same share on the prototype (new_x = x · distance_shape / (|x| + horiz_dist), step 2). A RAC halfway between the centre and the edge of its shoe lands halfway between the centre and the edge of the prototype.

The new shoes use the old prototype, so both models live in one coordinate system. Without it the maps could not be compared pixel by pixel, the old-against-new test (T6) would be impossible, and Part 2, which applies the old model to the new shoes, could not run. The new collection's own prototype is used only to clean its images (stickers and frame lines).

Why the maps differ

Part of the difference is how the pictures are drawn (above). Part is real: the shape test is significant (shoe bootstrap W = 46.7, p = 0.0056) and the goodness of fit rejects exact transfer. The new/old ratio of the two maps has a median of 1.11 and lies between 0.84 and 1.44 on 90% of the shoe, and the overall level is not significantly different (ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.93–1.22). The data point to four causes; they cannot tell which one matters most.

CauseEvidence
A different mix of sole designsA post-hoc group of 392 new shoes (probably one design) prints a band at the front of the heel but has only about 0.3 of its own RAC density there; one surface sits between this group and the rest.
A different collectionAnother source, another scan format (255 × 367 against 307 × 395), and probably another marking rule: on the 67 reprinted soles, the same RACs carry the same type code only 65% of the time.
Wear or markingNew shoes vary less between shoes (σ² 0.64 against 0.98, with the offset); σ² reflects both wear and marking.
A smoothing too coarse for the new dataCross-validation by shoe prefers a finer basis along the shoe on new, not on old. T5 found that the heel-front misfit comes mainly from this: with a finer basis its observed/expected goes to 1.04.

For the paper: this is Reviewer 1's point 4 and the editor's sole-design point. One surface for all shoes is an approximation, and RAC locations depend partly on the sole design.

About 67 new shoes are very likely reprints of old shoes and 22 more are uncertain, 15.8% of the new RACs. Consecutive new ids map onto consecutive old ids far more often than chance (16 of 57 pairs, where about 0.3 would be expected). The evidence comes from a screen of 121 flagged shoes, not of all new shoes.

Please confirm with Sarena or Yoram. The validation uses 478 shoes: not reprints, not uncertain, and passing the quality rule.

Part 1: snake and model on the new shoes

All 631 contours were built. An image reviewer checked sheets of every shoe three times (initial ellipse, first snake, final snake, prototype, cleaned shoe; docs/qa/sheets_new/). Stickers and frame lines were erased; 23 shoes received a fallback snake and shoe 170 its own ellipse. Quality matches the old shoes.

Reproducibility. After every step the old pipeline still reproduces the committed files exactly: bit for bit on Windows, where they were produced, and byte for byte between WSL reruns.

Part 2: goodness of fit on the new file

As Micha asked: for each new shoe, sum p·S over each part of the shoe with the old-fitted GLMM and the random effect at 0, scaled to the shoe's observed number of RACs. The parts are Naomi's 14 areas and grids of 10, 15 and 20 cells. The p-value comes from a two-sample shoe bootstrap (B = 2,000) that includes the old estimation error; a naive χ² with fixed expected counts would reject a correct model about 80% of the time.

ResultValue

Why, part (b): a shift along the shoeRecalibration removes only 9% of X². More RACs at the rear midfoot, fewer in the central forefoot.

Micha's grid: 10 to 20 cells on the standardized shoe

The cells are cut on the standardized shoe from the old shoes only, before any new number was computed: five bands from heel to toe, each holding 20% of the old contact area, and each band cut across into 2, 3 or 4 cells, giving 10, 15 or 20 cells (15 was chosen in advance as the main grid). In each cell, p·S is summed over the new shoes with the random effect at 0 and compared with the RACs observed there.

On Naomi's areas the old GLMM is too low at the heel and the rear midfoot (1.09 to 1.24) and too high in the central forefoot (0.74 and 0.82, the two blue areas in the middle of the forefoot). On every grid the pattern is the same: the heel bands are red (1.08 to 1.25) and the forefoot band blue (0.75 to 0.87). The 2022 model shows the same pattern a little more weakly, and is rejected on every grid too.

Where the old surface misses

A part with a point above 1 has more RACs on the new shoes than the old surface predicts. On Naomi's areas the old GLMM under-predicts the rear and heel areas (2, 9, 10: 13–24% more RACs than expected) and over-predicts the central ball and forefoot (12, 13, 14: 16–26% fewer). On the grids: above 1 in the two rear bands, lowest in band 4, back near 1 at the toe. This is the shift along the shoe that the goodness-of-fit test detects.

Is the test itself right?

A simulation on real shoe structure, with the model true, 400 replicates:

  • Pass. The goodness-of-fit test rejects a true model 5.2% of the time at the 5% level, so its p-values are valid.
  • Pass. The intervals that include the old estimation error are conservative (99.3–99.5% coverage).
  • Fail. The per-RAC log-score interval for the published surfaces covers 91% instead of 95%. The per-shoe lead interval above is therefore slightly optimistic.

Other findings for the paper

  • Knots. The 5 knots along the shoe are too coarse for the new data. This supports reporting a knot sensitivity analysis (meeting issue 8.4).
  • Naomi's 2022 estimator. optim with the default Nelder-Mead stops at its iteration limit, so its intensities are up to 9.8% from the optimum. This is immaterial for her conclusions (1.61 log-likelihood units), but she should know.
  • Wald and vcov. W is 428.7 with the Hessian vcov and 427.8 with the RX vcov. State the method in the paper.

Suggested reply to Reviewer 1

Points 1 and 6, to discuss.

We validated the model on an independent collection of 631 shoe prints (478 after excluding reprints of the original shoes). The spatial non-uniformity replicates strongly (Wald p < 10−16, model-based; it also holds with a cluster-robust variance). The fitted surface transfers only partly: a goodness-of-fit test that accounts for estimation error rejects exact transfer (p = 0.0005), and the shapes differ in a few bands, while the overall level is not significantly different (ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.93–1.22). Per RAC, the continuous surface predicts as well as the 2022 regional model, and per shoe the published surface is slightly better, although this lead is not established once the estimation error of the original fit is included. RACs within a shoe are not independent: pairs at short range are about 40% more frequent than expected. We therefore present the model as a description of where single RACs tend to occur, not as a tool to compute the probability of a set of RACs. We discuss sole design and dataset differences as limitations.
